37560.etyen:
Borrowed from Danish medister, from Middle Low German metworst (“sausage made from minced pork”), remodelled under the influence of ister (“suet, visceral fat”).
The Middle Low German compound consists of met (“pork”) and worst (“sausage”). The first element ultimately derives from Proto-Germanic *matją (“food”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“to drip, ooze; grease, fat”). The second element is from Proto-West Germanic *wursti (“sausage”), of uncertain further origin.
Compare German Mett and Dutch met (“minced pork”). The first element is also related to Norwegian Bokmål mat (“food”), Norw

Støre conveyed Norway's support for Magyar's ambitions to restore democracy and the rule of law in Hungary.

1000632.etyen:
Borrowed from German Ungarn (“Hungary”). The German name ultimately reflects Proto-Slavic *ǫgъrinъ (“Hungarian person”), of uncertain origin. The Proto-Slavic ethnonym may have been borrowed from the Oghuric name of the Onoğurs, probably meaning “ten tribes”, from 𐰆𐰣 (on, “ten”) and 𐰆𐰍𐰔 (oɣuz, “tribe”). Alternatively, it may have been borrowed from an early stage of Proto-Permic. The initial h- in forms such as English Hungary and French Hongrie arose through secondary association with the Huns.
Compare the related forms Danish Ungarn, Swedish Ungern, Faroese Ungarn, Finnish Unkari, Estonian U

en.g: the terrorist attacks carried out in Norway on 22 July 2011, comprising a bombing in the government quarter in Oslo and a mass shooting on Utøya
x: 22. juli har satt dype spor i det norske samfunnet.
The 22 July attacks have left deep marks on Norwegian society.
For den norske generasjonen bak meg er det 22. juli.
For the Norwegian generation behind me, it is 22 July.

1004472.etyen: From the calendar date 22. juli (“22 July”), read aloud as tjueandre juli (“the twenty-second of July”). Following the terrorist attacks of 22 July 2011, the date became a metonymic designation for the events themselves. The attacks consisted of a bombing in Regjeringskvartalet in Oslo and a mass shooting at the AUF summer camp on Utøya, killing 77 people.

1004728.etyen:
An old river name, probably related to kinn (“cheek; steep mountainside”), referring to the steep sides of Husedalen. The older genitival form Kinns is preserved as the first element of Kinsarvik, literally “the bay of Kinso”.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Kinso (“river”).

1004984.etyen:
Compound of à la grecque (“in the Greek style or manner”) + bord (“ornamental border”), literally “Greek-style border”.
The first element, à la grecque (“in the Greek style or manner”), is an unadapted borrowing from French à la grecque (“in the Greek manner”). It ultimately contains Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (“beyond, other”) through French la (“the”). The further origin of Γραικός (Graikós, “Graecian, Greek”), underlying French grecque (“Greek”), is uncertain.
The second element, bord (“ornamental border”), is borrowed from Middle Low German bōrde (“border, edge, hem”), from Proto-West Germ
